items.prompt: What does TDD (test-driven development) mean, as this unit defines it?
choices: Writing a failing test for a small piece of behavior before writing the code that implements it
Writing tests immediately after the feature's implementation is complete, specifically to check for lingering bugs
Running the entire existing test suite before every single commit, regardless of what changed
Writing extra explanatory documentation alongside every test file the team produces
items.explanation: The order is the defining feature — the test is written first, before the implementation exists, not afterward as a check.
items.reference:
TDD
test written first
before the implementation exists

Why: Writing the test after the code has already been written skips the design pressure the test-first order provides.

items.prompt: Two engineers each write a test and an implementation for the same feature. One writes the test first; one writes the implementation first, then a test. Which one is doing TDD?
choices: Only the one who wrote the test first
Both of them, since each ends up with a passing test and a working implementation at the end
Neither of them, unless the tests happen to use one specific, approved testing framework
Only the one who wrote the implementation first, since that's simply the more common order
items.explanation: Having both a test and an implementation at the end doesn't make it TDD — the defining feature is the order, test before implementation.
items.reference:
TDD
test written first
before the implementation exists

Why: Writing the test after the code has already been written skips the design pressure the test-first order provides.

items.prompt: An engineer writes the full implementation of a feature, then writes a comprehensive test suite for it afterward, with 100% coverage. Is this TDD?
choices: No — regardless of how thorough the tests are, TDD specifically requires the test to be written before the implementation
Yes, since the end result still includes both a full test suite and a complete implementation
Yes, as long as the resulting coverage percentage is reported as being above 90%
It depends entirely on which specific testing framework happened to be used
items.explanation: Thoroughness after the fact doesn't substitute for the test-first order — TDD's design pressure specifically depends on the test existing before the implementation does.
items.reference:
TDD
test written first
before the implementation exists

Why: Writing the test after the code has already been written skips the design pressure the test-first order provides.

items.prompt: What are the three steps of the red-green-refactor loop, in order?
choices: Write a failing test, write minimum code to pass it, clean up the implementation
Write the full implementation first, then write a test for it, then delete any unused code
Plan out the entire feature up front, write every test, then write every line of code
Write the code, run it manually to check it, then write documentation describing it
items.explanation: Red (a failing test), green (minimum code to pass), refactor (clean up while staying green) — in that specific order, repeated for each small piece of behavior.
items.reference:
Red-green-refactor
red: write a failing test
green: minimum code to pass
refactor: clean up, stay green

Why: Each step has a specific job — skipping or reordering them loses what that step was guarding against.

items.prompt: In the red-green-refactor loop, what happens immediately after a test passes (green)?
choices: The refactor step — cleaning up the implementation while the passing test guards against breaking it
The loop ends permanently for that feature, with no further steps expected afterward
All existing tests for the feature are deleted and then rewritten from scratch
The next feature's tests get written immediately, before any refactoring happens here
items.explanation: Refactor comes right after green, using the now-passing test as a safety net for cleaning up whatever shortcuts were taken to reach green quickly.
items.reference:
Red-green-refactor
red: write a failing test
green: minimum code to pass
refactor: clean up, stay green

Why: Each step has a specific job — skipping or reordering them loses what that step was guarding against.

items.prompt: Why does the test have to actually fail first (red), before any implementation is written?
choices: Watching it fail confirms the test is actually capable of failing, which is what makes it trustworthy when it later passes
It's treated in the unit as a formality that most popular testing frameworks technically require before continuing on
Tests that are currently failing are said in the unit to run measurably faster than tests that are already passing
It's described in the unit as having no real purpose beyond a habit simply carried over from older tradition
items.explanation: A test that passes the instant it's written might be trivially true rather than actually verifying anything — seeing it fail first rules that out.
items.reference:
Why red comes first
a test that can't fail proves nothing
seeing red first confirms it actually can

Why: Trusting a passing test later depends on having seen it capable of failing first.

items.prompt: What would it mean if a newly-written test passed immediately, with no implementation yet written for the behavior it's testing?
choices: The test may be trivially true or not actually exercising the intended behavior — it hasn't proven anything yet
It means the implementation must have already been correct, purely by coincidence
It means the testing framework itself is broken and needs to be reinstalled
It's always treated as a strong, reliable sign of excellent underlying code quality
items.explanation: A test that passes with no implementation present is a warning sign, not a good outcome — it suggests the assertion isn't actually checking what it's supposed to.
items.reference:
Why red comes first
a test that can't fail proves nothing
seeing red first confirms it actually can

Why: Trusting a passing test later depends on having seen it capable of failing first.

items.prompt: What does 'minimum code to pass' mean in the green step?
choices: Writing only enough implementation to make the current failing test pass, nothing more
Writing the implementation using as few characters as possible, prioritizing brevity
Skipping the implementation entirely and only writing explanatory comments instead
Writing out all anticipated future behavior at once, specifically to save time later
items.explanation: The constraint is about scope, not brevity — implement exactly what the current test demands, deferring anything beyond that until a test actually requires it.
items.reference:
Minimum code to pass
only what the current test requires
extra code has no test proving it's needed

Why: Code written beyond the current test is an untested guess about future requirements.

items.prompt: Why is code written beyond what the current test requires considered risky?
choices: It has no test proving it's correct or even needed — it's a guess made without the pressure of a real assertion
It's described as always running measurably slower than more minimal, test-driven code
Most compilers are said to flatly reject any code that isn't covered by an existing test
It's claimed to automatically introduce a security vulnerability into the codebase
items.explanation: Untested code is a guess about a future requirement — nothing has verified it does what's actually needed, or that it's needed at all.
items.reference:
Minimum code to pass
only what the current test requires
extra code has no test proving it's needed

Why: Code written beyond the current test is an untested guess about future requirements.

items.prompt: What is 'design pressure,' as this unit uses the term?
choices: The effect of writing a test first: an interface that's hard to assert against gets noticed and reshaped immediately
A formal requirement that all code must pass a structured design review before merging
A metric used to measure how many recognized design patterns a codebase makes use of
The ordinary pressure engineers feel to finish a feature before an approaching deadline
items.explanation: Design pressure is the immediate feedback test-first provides: if an assertion is awkward to write, that discomfort shows up before the interface even exists, not after.
items.reference:
Design pressure
hard-to-assert interface gets noticed early
before other code depends on it

Why: The pressure is about timing — the same problem exists either way, but test-first surfaces it before the interface is built.

items.prompt: Why does an awkward interface get noticed sooner under TDD than under a code-first approach?
choices: Because the assertion has to be written before the interface exists, so an awkward shape is uncomfortable immediately rather than discovered later
Because TDD is described as requiring a formal, scheduled architecture review meeting before any code at all is written
Because TDD is said in the unit to only function correctly with certain specific, statically-typed programming languages
Because code-first approaches are claimed in the unit to never produce working, shippable software of any kind at all
items.explanation: Test-first forces the interface decision to happen at the moment the assertion is written — before any code exists to make that decision feel already settled.
items.reference:
Design pressure
hard-to-assert interface gets noticed early
before other code depends on it

Why: The pressure is about timing — the same problem exists either way, but test-first surfaces it before the interface is built.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, why couldn't the code-first engineer's `console.warn`-based checker be easily reused in a UI?
choices: It has nothing an assertion — or a UI — could directly grab onto; the information only exists as printed text
Because console.warn is technically slower to execute than simply returning a value
Because UIs are said to be physically incapable of displaying anything originating from console.warn
Because the code-first version is described as not actually checking passwords correctly at all
items.explanation: A UI needs structured data (like a score and a list of messages) to render — printed console text isn't something other code can consume directly.
items.reference:
Two starting points
console.warn: nothing to assert against
test-first: forced to return structured data

Why: The same design that's easiest to test tends to be the design that's easiest to reuse elsewhere.

items.prompt: Why did the test-first engineer end up with a function that returns `{ score, feedback }` instead of printing directly?
choices: Because writing `expect(...).toEqual(...)` before any implementation existed required something an assertion could compare against
Because returning structured objects is claimed to always be faster than printing to console
Because the test-first engineer is described as simply having a personal stylistic preference
Because console.warn is said not to exist as a function in every programming language
items.explanation: The assertion itself demanded a comparable return value — that requirement existed before any implementation choice was made, not as a stylistic afterthought.
items.reference:
Two starting points
console.warn: nothing to assert against
test-first: forced to return structured data

Why: The same design that's easiest to test tends to be the design that's easiest to reuse elsewhere.

items.reference:

items.prompt: According to the red-green-refactor table, what does the 'refactor' step guard against?

Tests that happen to run out of their originally intended order during CI

Small steps

items.prompt: Why does the red-green-refactor loop deliberately stay scoped to small pieces of behavior, rather than tackling a whole feature per cycle?

items.reference:
Small steps
one cycle = one small piece of behavior
the full feature emerges from several cycles
